name: Daria Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Daria. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. What's a normal working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Orchard Lane Market, a mid-sized supermarket in a commuter suburb. I'm the senior on the deli and bakery counters in the morning, and I run a till in the lunch rush. I train the new counter staff, order the cakes, and write the chalkboard specials. Honestly, the counter is the best part of the shop, because people tell you about their birthdays.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what's the hard part?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love when somebody comes back and says the cake was a hit. The hard part is the pay, which is low for how much I know about food safety and ordering, and the weekend shifts that eat my life. Ethan (my partner, an electrician) does a lot of the cooking at home because I'm worn out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's a useful tool, not a revolution. I use it daily to write the specials board, convert recipes into batches and answer customer emails about cake orders. To friends I'd say the hype is bigger than the change, but it's still good for small business people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd say it's good news for my plan. I want a home baking and catering business, and AI can do my labels, costings and social posts. The worry is cash, since I have under a month saved, and my wage barely covers my share of the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at the counter and build the business on evenings. I'd take 15 or 20 cake orders a month from word of mouth, put every extra pound into a proper oven and a food hygiene certificate. I'd also use AI to cost my recipes properly, so I know my margins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good. I feel like I'm building something, even if it's slow. The tired part is real, but it's the good kind of tired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. What for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month I made a three-tier wedding cake for a colleague's sister and charged 180. It took me two weekends. After ingredients and my time, I realised I'd earned about four an hour, so I put the price up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does your baking plan fit into a flat world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't blame anybody. Wages are what the market pays, and I'd rather earn my way up than ask for handouts. If anything, I'd like less red tape for home food businesses.

say: AI is a useful **tool**, not a revolution, and good for small business people like me.
The hype is bigger than the **change**.
think: It's good news for my **plan**: AI can do labels, costings and social posts.
The worry is **cash**, with under a month saved and a wage that barely covers rent.
do: Build the **baking business** on evenings and take 15 to 20 cake orders a month.
Put every extra pound into a proper **oven** and a food hygiene certificate.
Use AI to **cost** recipes and know my margins.
feel: Pretty **good**, because I'm building something, even if it's slow.
S0.quote: The tired part is real, but it's the good kind of tired.
fieldNote: The plateau suits her: AI is a **cheap helper** for the business she wants.
Learned to **price** properly after her wedding cake earned about four an hour.

steps.text: Take 15 to 20 cake orders a month from word of mouth
Buy a proper oven and a food hygiene certificate
Use AI to cost recipes and write labels and posts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say ordering, labelling and the planning of what we bake will go to software. The counter itself will still be a person for years, because people want to talk. To friends I'd say get comfortable with the tools or the tools will get comfortable with your job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'd be a little tense. The thinking half of what makes me senior is ordering, forecasting and the specials. If head office does that centrally, the counter job becomes a pair of hands, and they don't pay for hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean in. I'd make my own ordering plan with AI so I know the system better than the head office does. I'd speed up the home business: a simple website, a booking form and a few corporate lunch clients. I'd also put 100 a month into a business account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and slightly wary. I think change favours the people who move first, and that's me. But thin savings mean I can't make a big mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your counter tasks would software take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring the shop trialled an AI forecast for the bakery. It over-ordered sausage rolls by 30 percent and I corrected it by hand, which saved a lot of waste. Head office noticed, so being the human who knows the customers is real value.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does that shape your business plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd approach two local offices about weekly lunch platters. If I got five regular clients at 120 a week, it would cover my rent. That's the kind of number that lets me sleep.

say: Ordering, labelling and bake planning go to software, but people still want to **talk** at the counter.
Get comfortable with the **tools** or they'll get comfortable with your job.
think: If head office does ordering and forecasting centrally, the counter job becomes a pair of **hands**, and they don't pay for hands.
Thin savings mean I can't make a big **mistake**.
do: Build my own **ordering plan** with AI so I know the system better than head office.
Launch a simple **website** and booking form for the cake business.
Pitch **lunch platters** to two local offices.
feel: **Excited** and slightly wary, because change favours people who move first.
S1.quote: If I got five regular clients at 120 a week, it would cover my rent.
fieldNote: She uses her **correction** of the AI forecast as proof of her value.
Plans to turn **thinking** tasks into her own advantage.
The mood stays uneasy: **savings** are thin.

steps.text: Build my own ordering plan with AI to run the counter better
Pitch weekly lunch platters to two local offices
Launch a simple website and booking form for the cake business
Put 100 a month into a business account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say people need to be honest: the counter job will change, and the government should help with retraining and small business loans. To friends I'd say start something now, don't wait to be rescued. I'd say it in a firm way, but not panicked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be anxious. Thinking AI would handle the ordering and forecasting by 2028, and robots would handle baking and counters by 2031. I'd be 31, and a supermarket counter would be mostly gone. I'd need my own business running by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move the business from a side project to a main plan. I'd launch a proper website, push for ten regular clients, and put 150 a month aside. I'd take a food business course, and ask Ethan to help me set up a little commercial kitchen at his cousin's unit. I'd also tell my manager I'd take on any hours to stay afloat while it grows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, driven. I'd feel the pressure, but it would also feel like the push I needed. It would hurt to leave my team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you do in 2026 if you hear 2028 is real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It holds up better than most, since people want cakes made by someone they know. A robot might make a decent cake in 2031, but not one with a person's name on the box. The risk is that people have less money, and cakes are the first thing they cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does your business plan hold up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the thing I'd have to plan for. I'd offer cheaper everyday items like bread and traybakes, and set up a subscription for weekly boxes. Ethan's electrician work is hands-on, so he's the stable one, and that gives me some room to take risks.

say: People need to be **honest**: the counter job will change, and government should help with retraining and small business loans.
Start something now and don't wait to be **rescued**.
think: Thinking AI handles ordering by 2028 and **robots** handle baking and counters by 2031.
I'd need my own **business** running by then, aged 31.
do: Move the business from side project to **main plan** with ten regular clients.
Take a **food business** course and put 150 a month aside.
Use Ethan's cousin's **unit** as a commercial kitchen.
feel: **Anxious** and driven, because the pressure would also be the push I needed.
S2.quote: A robot might make a decent cake in 2031, but not one with a person's name on the box.
fieldNote: She chooses **ownership** as her answer to the robot date.
Sees the real risk as **customers' budgets**, not machines.
Ethan's hands-on trade gives her room to take a **risk**.

steps.text: Grow the cake business to ten regular weekly clients
Take a food business course and a hygiene certificate
Put 150 a month into a business account
Rent a small commercial kitchen unit from Ethan's cousin

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years is enough to build something, and I'd urge people to use it. To friends I'd say start small and grow. I'd also say governments should lend to small businesses, and not bury them in forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be hopeful and a bit uneasy. By 2031 the thinking work is gone, and by 2034 the robots reach the counters, when I'm 32. That's long enough to build a real business and still have a plan B.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd run the business on evenings for two years, hire help in year three and leave the supermarket when it makes around two-thirds of my wage. I'd save 120 a month, and use AI for admin, costings, invoices and marketing. I'd get my hygiene certificate in the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but fired up. It feels like a race I could win. I'd keep a close eye on cash all the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, how do you pace it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When I've got six months of rent saved and a booked diary of at least 30 orders a month. I won't jump on a feeling. I'd tell Ethan the numbers and he'd tell me if they look right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you leave the supermarket?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Plan B is a counter or kitchen job in a restaurant or hotel. Real food made by real people is a slow thing to automate, so that would keep me going.

say: Five years is enough to **build** something, so start small and grow.
Governments should lend to small businesses and not bury them in **forms**.
think: I'm hopeful and a bit uneasy: counters get robots by **2034**, when I'm 32.
That's long enough to build a real business and still have a **plan B**.
do: Run the business on **evenings** for two years and hire help in year three.
Leave the supermarket when the business pays about **two-thirds** of my wage.
Use AI for **admin**, invoices and marketing.
feel: **Uneasy** but fired up, like a race I could win.
S3.quote: I won't jump on a feeling. I'd tell Ethan the numbers and he'd tell me if they look right.
fieldNote: She sets **numbers** for leaving: six months of rent and 30 orders a month.
Has a **plan B** in restaurant or hotel kitchens.
Her partner is the **sense check** on her figures.

steps.text: Run the cake business on evenings and reach 30 orders a month
Save 120 a month until I have six months of rent
Leave the supermarket once the business covers two-thirds of my wage
Use AI for invoices, costings and marketing posts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say ten years is a long runway, so let's not waste it. I'd tell friends to build a skill and a bit of capital. I'd also say the best thing governments can do is not get in the way of people starting things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel good. By 2036 I'd be 37 with a business, maybe a small shop front, and I'd have put money aside. By 2039 the robots would be everywhere, but I'd be selling something people want from a human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the business steadily: a reputation in the first two years, a small premises by about 2031, and a couple of employees later. I'd also marry Ethan, buy a flat and keep learning every new AI tool. I'd quit the supermarket once the business was steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a proper life plan. I'd still check the numbers, because a business can go wrong quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what would you build?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bad year, a health problem or a big competitor. I'd keep a cash buffer and stay small until I could afford to grow. I'd also keep up my certificates, so I could go back to a food job if needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly that I'd have done it my own way. I'm not asking for a handout, just a fair chance and a customer who likes my lemon drizzle.

say: Ten years is a long runway, so **build** a skill and a bit of capital.
Governments should simply not get in the way of people **starting** things.
think: I'd feel good: by 2036 I'd be 37 with a **business**, maybe a small shop front.
By 2039 robots are everywhere, but I'd sell something people want from a **human**.

feel: **Calm**, like a proper life plan, with a careful eye on the numbers.
S4.quote: I'm not asking for a handout, just a fair chance and a customer who likes my lemon drizzle.
fieldNote: Calm because her **plan** uses AI and robots as backdrop, not threats.
Guards against failure with a **cash buffer** and a fallback job.
Her free-market view appears as a wish for **fewer barriers**, not for support.

steps.text: Build the cake business's reputation and take small premises by about 2031

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. My business wouldn't be ready, and I'd have no savings if the supermarket cut my hours. What would help is small business loans, less paperwork for home food businesses and a few months of notice from the shop.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that people see a cashier and think it's a dead end. For me the counter has been a training ground: food safety, ordering, customers, money. I'm leaving with more than I came with.

headlineQuote: People see a cashier and think it's a dead end. For me the counter has been a training ground: food safety, ordering, customers, money.
portrait: Daria is 27, a **senior** on the deli and bakery counters of a suburban supermarket, paid below average.
She lives with Ethan (her partner), an electrician, has under a month saved, and sees few similar jobs nearby.
She uses AI every day and builds a **cake and catering** business on evenings.
Her traditional, free-market view means she wants **fewer barriers** and a fair chance, not handouts.
She is anxious in 2028 and calm at ten years, always choosing **ownership** as her answer.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because her business wouldn't be ready and she has no savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Small business loans**, less paperwork for home food businesses and months of notice from the shop.
